“It crashed again.” Reena leaned in close. “Devika, don't tell me. Let me read it.”
“Go on.”
“IndexError, list index out of range, line fourteen.” Reena frowned. “Line fourteen. Not line one, so the whole program isn't wrong.”
“Where's the list?”
“Line nine. Five items.” Reena counted under the breath. “And the loop goes up to six. Off by one?”
“Maybe. How could you check?”
“Comment out the bottom half first. If it runs, the trouble is down there.” Reena typed hash marks. The program ran. “Okay, bottom half.” Reena changed the six to a five and ran it. “One change. Works.”
Devika smiled. “Only one?”
“One at a time, or I'll never know which fixed it.”

qa.q: Which line did the error message point to?
What might Reena be feeling when asking Devika not to tell the answer?
qa.a: Determined and a little proud: Reena wants to work it out alone 🙂.

qa.q: What could Reena do if the error came back after the fix, and why?
qa.a: Print the values inside the loop and change one thing at a time, since checking after every change shows which change matters.

qa.q: How does Reena's approach look to Devika?
qa.a: Devika, who only asks questions, sees Reena reasoning step by step, and may feel it is better to let Reena find the fix than to hand it over.

grounding: A teen faced with a crash reads the error, isolates the cause by commenting out half the code and fixes one thing at a time.

passage:
The crash came at eleven at night, the evening before I'd promised Pallavi the timetable maker. I'm Sharmila, and back then my first instinct was to change random lines until something worked.
That night I made myself read the red text instead. The first line named the part called make_slots. The next gave line forty-two. The last said a list index was out of range. So, I thought, something is asking for a slot that doesn't exist. But which part feeds it?
I put a hash in front of every line in the bottom half so it wouldn't run. No crash. The problem lived in that half. I brought it back a few lines at a time, running after each. It broke when the Saturday part returned: I'd given Saturday four periods, but its list only had three. One fix, one run, and it worked. I remember feeling almost calm, which surprised me.

qa.q: What did the last line of the error say?
qa.a: It said a list index was out of range.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel once the fix worked, and why was that a surprise?
qa.a: Sharmila felt almost calm, which was surprising, since the old habit under late-night pressure was changing random lines in a panic.

qa.q: What else could Sharmila do if hiding half the code had not explained the crash?
qa.a: Add print lines that show what each list holds just before the crash, so the real values reveal which assumption is wrong.

qa.q: How is Pallavi affected by the way Sharmila handled the crash?
qa.a: Pallavi gets the timetable maker on time and working, instead of a rushed version patched with random changes that might break again.

grounding: Shows a teen's reasoning while debugging: reading the error, switching off half the code to find the fault, then fixing and rechecking one change at a time.

Computer club observation, Friday
Imran's weather logger crashed three times before the break. Last month he would have called me over at once. Today I stayed at my desk and listened, because he was talking it through with Harsha, who sits beside him.
“Okay, it says ‘cannot convert string to number’. So somewhere I'm doing maths on text.” He scrolled to the line the message named. “That's the average. So the temperatures are text. Where do they come from?” He hid the averaging part with comment marks and printed the list instead. The numbers came out wrapped in quote marks. “There. They come in from the file as words.” He changed one line to convert them, ran it, then checked the average by hand on Harsha's calculator.
Next step for me: ask Imran to show this method to the Monday beginners.

qa.q: What did the error message say?
qa.a: It said "cannot convert string to number".

qa.q: What does Imran's talking aloud suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: It suggests he felt steady and in control rather than panicked, following each clue in turn instead of calling for help at once.

qa.q: How could the club build on what Imran did?
qa.a: Having Imran walk the Monday beginners through reading one real error and isolating it would show them a method, not just a fix.

qa.q: What is it like for Harsha to sit beside Imran during this?
qa.a: Harsha hears the reasoning step by step and even helps check the average, so the crash becomes a shared lesson rather than a private struggle.

grounding: Shows a teen thinking aloud while debugging: reading the error, isolating the failing part, fixing one line and checking the result.
